issues.legal_issue: A reasoned government policy adopted in the public interest to prevent private monopolisation may override a contractual right to participate in future port tenders without a separate legislative measure.
material_facts: The licence agreements granted operators rights to participate in future tenders, while other terms restricted bidding for additional facilities.

The government changed its policy to prevent concentration of control over port facilities and promote competition, including by excluding an existing operator from the immediately following tender while permitting participation in a later tender.
The policy was directed at risks to competition and the shipping industry, including the ability of operators to favour their own ships and affect access to port facilities.
The Court found no arbitrariness in the policy change and considered the larger public interest it served.
issues.conclusion: The policy was a valid exercise of government power and could prevail over contractual bid rights; a policy change for this purpose did not require legislation, provided it was reasoned and non-arbitrary.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, courts ordinarily do not interfere with government policy unless it is arbitrary or constitutionally infirm. The government may change policy with changing circumstances, and a reasoned policy serving the general public interest may override private contractual rights. The change must be free from arbitrariness, irrationality, bias and malice and satisfy Wednesbury reasonableness. The Court relied on Shimnit Utsch India Private Ltd. v. West Bengal Transport Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. and the earlier P&O Ports litigation, in which exclusion of an existing operator to prevent monopolisation had been upheld.

rule.if: port_tender_eligibility_challenge and contract_grants_future_bid_right and policy_serves_public_interest and policy_has_reasoned_competition_basis and policy_is_non_arbitrary

predicates.port_tender_eligibility_challenge: An operator challenged its exclusion from a public tender for port facilities.
predicates.contract_grants_future_bid_right: The operator's contract granted it a right to participate in future tenders.
predicates.policy_serves_public_interest: The government adopted the policy to protect the public interest in the use and operation of port facilities.
predicates.policy_has_reasoned_competition_basis: The policy was based on promoting competition and preventing private concentration of control over port facilities.
predicates.policy_is_non_arbitrary: The Court found the policy change to be reasoned and not arbitrary.

issues.definition: When an operator challenges tender exclusion despite a contractual right to bid, a reasoned and non-arbitrary policy serving the public interest in competition may override that right.

issues.legal_issue: An operator excluded from one tender under a policy restricting participation in successive tenders cannot be excluded from the next tender merely because delay in completing the earlier tender caused the next tender to be treated as the excluded tender.
material_facts: The operator had been excluded from bidding for the third container terminal under the existing policy.
The tender for that terminal had not been finalised when the tender for the fourth terminal was issued.
The authorities treated the fourth terminal tender as the third terminal tender and excluded the operator again.

The Court found that the operator was entitled under the revised policy to participate in alternate bids and that excluding it from the fourth tender would apply a different yardstick after it had already been excluded from one bid.
issues.conclusion: The operator could continue participating in the tender for the fourth container terminal, and the decision excluding it was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: A tenderer already excluded from one bid under a policy permitting participation in alternate bids cannot be excluded from the next bid on a different yardstick because of fortuitous delay in finalising the earlier tender; doing so would be contrary to public policy.

rule.if: port_tender_disqualification_challenge and tenderer_excluded_from_one_bid and earlier_tender_unfinalised and later_tender_treated_as_earlier_tender

predicates.port_tender_disqualification_challenge: An operator challenged its exclusion from a later public tender for port facilities.
predicates.tenderer_excluded_from_one_bid: The operator had already been excluded from participation in one tender under the applicable participation policy.
predicates.earlier_tender_unfinalised: The tender from which the operator had been excluded had not been finalised when another tender was issued.
predicates.later_tender_treated_as_earlier_tender: The authorities treated the later tender as the earlier tender and relied on that treatment to exclude the operator again.

issues.definition: Where an operator has already been excluded from one bid and an unfinished earlier tender leads the authorities to treat a later tender as that same bid, the operator may participate in the later tender.

issues.legal_issue: A legitimate expectation based on a contractual right to bid does not prevent exclusion under a reasoned policy adopted in the public interest unless the government action amounts to an abuse of power.
material_facts: The operator relied on contractual clauses allowing it to participate in future tenders and on its prior participation in the tender process.
The government adopted a policy to prevent port facilities from being concentrated in the hands of a private group or consortium and to promote competition.
The Court found that the policy served the public interest and that the decision to exclude the operator was not arbitrary or unreasonable.
issues.conclusion: The asserted legitimate expectation did not warrant interference with the exclusion decision, and the challenge to that decision was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: As explained in Sethi Auto Service Station v. Delhi Development Authority, legitimate expectation has no role where state action is based on public policy and public interest, unless the action amounts to an abuse of power. A change in policy may defeat a substantive legitimate expectation if the change is justified by Wednesbury reasonableness.

rule.if: public_tender_exclusion_challenge and claimant_relies_on_prior_bid_expectation and policy_serves_public_interest and policy_change_is_reasoned and no_abuse_of_power

predicates.public_tender_exclusion_challenge: An operator challenged its exclusion from a public tender.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_prior_bid_expectation: The operator relied on a contractual right or prior treatment as creating an expectation of being permitted to bid.
predicates.policy_serves_public_interest: The government based its tender policy on a public interest in preventing concentration of control and promoting competition.
predicates.policy_change_is_reasoned: The government supported the policy change with reasons that satisfy the applicable standard of reasonableness.
predicates.no_abuse_of_power: The Court found no abuse of power in the government's action.

issues.definition: A tenderer's expectation based on a contractual right or prior treatment does not prevent a reasoned public-interest policy from supporting exclusion when the government's action is not an abuse of power.
